person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the YOLO family of real-time object detectors from v1 to v8, and the single number the whole family is ranked by
span.quote: We present a comprehensive analysis of YOLO’s evolution, examining the innovations and contributions in each iteration from the original YOLO up to YOLOv8, YOLO-NAS, and YOLO with transformers.

span.label: what changed architecturally at each YOLO iteration, and on what measure the improvements are quoted
span.quote: We present a comprehensive analysis of YOLO’s evolution, examining the innovations and contributions in each iteration from the original YOLO up to YOLOv8, YOLO-NAS, and YOLO with transformers.

span.label: a version-by-version account of the architecture changes, prefaced by an explanation of the evaluation metric that shows it is not one metric
span.quote: The AP is computed differently in the VOC and in the COCO datasets.

span.label: method
span.quote: The AP metric is based on precision–recall metrics, handling multiple object categories, and defining a positive prediction using Intersection over Union (IoU).

span.label: real-time object detection, whose published progress is stated almost entirely in points of AP
span.quote: Among the different object detection algorithms, the YOLO (You Only Look Once) framework has stood out for its remarkable balance of speed and accuracy, enabling the rapid and reliable identification of objects in images.

span.label: narrative review of each YOLO release, with a metrics section deriving AP for both the PASCAL VOC and the Microsoft COCO conventions
span.term: narrative review of each YOLO release, with a metrics section deriving AP for both the PASCAL VOC and the Microsoft COCO conventions
span.quote: The AP metric is based on precision–recall metrics, handling multiple object categories, and defining a positive prediction using Intersection over Union (IoU).

span.label: AP is built on the precision-recall curve, and precision and recall trade against each other - detecting more objects raises recall and produces more false positives - so the single number is an area under a curve, not a count
span.quote: There is often a tradeoff between precision and recall; for example, increasing the number of detected objects (higher recall) can result in more false positives (lower precision).

span.label: what counts as a correct detection at all is set by an IoU threshold, and COCO averages over a RANGE of thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95 - so the definition of `correct` is itself a parameter being averaged over
span.quote: It measures the overlap between the ground truth and predicted bounding boxes. The COCO benchmark considers multiple IoU thresholds to evaluate the model’s performance at different levels of localization accuracy.

span.label: TWO NAMES FOR ONE THING: `average precision (AP), TRADITIONALLY CALLED mean average precision (mAP)`, and `THE COCO DATASET MAKES NO DISTINCTION BETWEEN AP AND mAP`. The review has to declare which word it will use before it can use it
span.quote: The average precision (AP), traditionally called mean average precision (mAP), is the commonly used metric for evaluating the performance of object detection models. It measures the average precision across all categories, providing a single value to compare different models. The COCO dataset makes no distinction between AP and mAP. In the rest of this paper, we will refer to this metric as AP.

span.label: AND ONE NAME FOR TWO COMPUTATIONS: `The AP is computed differently in the VOC and in the COCO datasets` - 11-point interpolation over 20 categories at one IoU threshold, against 101-point interpolation over 80 categories averaged over ten IoU thresholds
span.quote: The AP is computed differently in the VOC and in the COCO datasets.

span.label: THE CONSEQUENCE IS STATED PLAINLY AND IT IS ABOUT COMPARABILITY: `the differences in AP calculation MAKE IT HARD TO DIRECTLY COMPARE the performance of object detection models across the two datasets`
span.quote: The differences in AP calculation make it hard to directly compare the performance of object detection models across the two datasets.

span.label: the improvements the field reports are quoted in that same word - 2.3 points from simOTA, 2.4 from stronger augmentation - so the increments inherit whatever the number means on the day
span.quote: YOLOX, inspired by this work, proposed a simplified version called simOTA. This change increased AP by 2.3 points.

span.label: the review derives AP separately for each dataset convention before reporting any model's score, rather than treating the metric as given
span.note: eliminates: a reader lining up a YOLOv2 number against a YOLOv5 number - the first is VOC AP and the second is COCO AP, and they are different quantities · outcome: held

span.quote: The average precision (AP), traditionally called mean average precision (mAP), is the commonly used metric for evaluating the performance of object detection models. It measures the average precision across all categories, providing a single value to compare different models. The COCO dataset makes no distinction between AP and mAP. In the rest of this paper, we will refer to this metric as AP.

span.label: AP, VOC SENSE - 11-point interpolation of the precision-recall curve, averaged over 20 categories, at a single IoU threshold
span.quote: This dataset includes 20 object categories. To compute the AP in VOC, we follow the next steps: - For each category, calculate the precision–recall curve by varying the confidence threshold of the model’s predictions. - Calculate each category’s average precision (AP) using an interpolated 11-point sampling of the precision–recall curve. - Compute the final average precision (AP) by taking the mean of the APs across all 20 categories.

span.label: AP, COCO SENSE - 101-point interpolation, 80 categories, averaged over IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05. THE SAME SYMBOL AS THE VOC SENSE AND A DIFFERENT QUANTITY, which is why numbers from the two eras of YOLO cannot be lined up
span.quote: This dataset includes 80 object categories and uses a more complex method for calculating AP. Instead of using an 11-point interpolation, it uses a 101-point interpolation, i.e., it computes the precision for 101 recall thresholds from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.01. Also, the AP is obtained by averaging over multiple IoU values instead of just one, except for a common AP metric called AP50, which is the AP for a single IoU threshold of 0.5.

span.label: AP50 - the one COCO figure that is a single-threshold measurement, named separately BECAUSE it is the exception. The existence of a special name for the simple case is the clearest sign that the unqualified word is not simple
